chunks: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from Ṣafwān ibn Mihrān al-Jammāl, who said:

I asked Abā ʿAbdِ اللَّهِ عليه السلام about the cisterns that are between Makkah and al-Madīnah, to which beasts come, dogs lap in them, donkeys drink from them, and from which the junub bathes and wudu is performed.
So he said: “And how much is the amount of the water?” I said: “Up to half the shin and up to the knee.” He said: “Perform wudu from it.”

Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: The proper way regarding these two reports and others of their kind is that we interpret them to mean that when the water is more than a kurr, then in such a case it is not rendered impure by what falls into it; and whenever it is less than a kurr, then it is rendered impure according to what we have stated.

key_terms.السِّبَاعُ: beasts or wild animals that come to the water
key_terms.الْجُنُبُ: a person in the state requiring ghusl due to janabah
key_terms.الْحِيَاضِ: cisterns or pools used to collect water
key_terms.قَدْرُ الْمَاءِ: the quantity or amount of the water
key_terms.كُرٍّ: the juridical measure of abundant water used in rulings of najasah

ai.seo_question: Can wudu be performed from pond or cistern water that animals drink from?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses the ruling of using water from roadside cisterns frequented by animals and used by people for bathing and wudu. Imam al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام permits wudu from such water in the described case, and Shaykh al-Ṭūsī explains the report in light of the juridical principle that water exceeding a kurr is not made najis by incidental contact with impurities.
